The suction-casting experiments were conducted with a water-cooled copper mold method. Firstly an appropriate amount of alloy was melted again in a quartz crucible in high vacuum with argon atmosphere. Then the remelted alloy was sucked into a copper mold, which has inner cavity with a size of 4 5m m /C2 80 mm and is cooled by high-speed water.

attributes.morphology: coarse black primary phase and lamellar plates
attributes.location: primary phase and within eutectic cell

evidence.quote: The microstructure of the conventionally cast NiAl–Cr(Mo)–Hf eutectic alloy (as shown in Fig. 1(a)) is composed of gray eutectic cell, black coarse NiAl phase and white phase which is mainly distributed at the eutectic cell boundaries.

attributes.morphology: coarser rods at intercellular zone and radially emanating plates in eutectic cell

evidence.quote: In the eutectic cell, black NiAl and gray Cr(Mo) plates exhibited a radially emanating pattern from the cell interior to its boundaries. Coarser Cr(Mo) rods, primary NiAl phase and white Ni 2AlHf phase are mainly distributed at the intercellular zone.

attributes.location: eutectic cell boundaries and intercellular zone

evidence.quote: According to the former research [6] the white phase should be Ni 2AlHf Heusler phase.

attributes.morphology: fine lamellar and fine primary phase

evidence.quote: The eutectic cell, NiAl/Cr(Mo) lamellar, primary NiAl phase and Ni 2AlHf precipitates become fine, and the Ni 2AlHf precipitates are semi-continuously distributed along the eutectic cell boundaries.
TEM observations show that there are some fine Cr(Mo) precipitates with size of 5–10 nm in the primary NiAl phase, as shown in Fig. 1 (e).
the Ni 2AlHf precipitates are semi-continuously distributed along the eutectic cell boundaries.
gray eutectic cell
In the eutectic cell, black NiAl and gray Cr(Mo) plates exhibited a radially emanating pattern from the cell interior to its boundaries.
The eutectic cell, NiAl/Cr(Mo) lamellar, primary NiAl phase and Ni 2AlHf precipitates become fine
The eutectic cell, NiAl/Cr(Mo) lamellar, primary NiAl phase and Ni 2AlHf precipitates become fine
Moreover high-density network dislocations along the NiAl/Cr(Mo) phase interface and fine NiAl and Cr(Mo) precipitates are observed in the suction-casting alloy, as shown in Fig. 1 (f).
The local degeneration of NiAl and Cr(Mo) lamellar near the eutectic cell boundary occurs and the eutectic morphology coarsens significantly.

The observations on the primary NiAl phase show that the Cr(Mo) precipitates tend to be coarse (as shown in Fig. 2(e)), which suggests that Cr and Mo elements solid solved in the NiAl phase precipitate during HIP treatment.

attributes.location: eutectic cell boundary and NiAl/Cr(Mo) interface

evidence.quote: The distribution of the Ni 2AlHf phase at the eutectic cell boundary becomes finer and the volume fraction of Ni 2AlHf phase at the intercellular region decreases. TEM investigations reveal that many fine Ni 2AlHf particles precipitate at NiAl/Cr(Mo) phase interface inside eutectic cell, as shown in Fig. 2 (b).

attributes.location: eutectic cell boundary and NiAl/Cr(Mo) interface

evidence.quote: The TEM observations also revealed Hf solid solution (Hfss) precipitates with hexagon or irregular shape, as shown in Fig. 2 (c) and (d). The EDS test on the Hfss finds that it contains more Cr elements, compared with Ni 2AlHf phase.
The local degeneration of NiAl and Cr(Mo) lamellar near the eutectic cell boundary occurs and the eutectic morphology coarsens significantly.
the TEM observations show that some dislocations extend into the NiAl phase in the HIP-treated suction-cast alloy, while almost no mobile dislocation exist in the Cr(Mo) lamellar
The plastic strain in compression and yield strength of the suction-cast alloy are about 16% and 1450 MPa respectively, which are significantly improved, compared with the conventionally cast alloy.
The plastic strain in compression and yield strength of the suction-cast alloy are about 16% and 1450 MPa respectively, which are significantly improved, compared with the conventionally cast alloy.

After the HIP treatment, the RT yield strength of the HIP-treated suction-cast alloy decreases, but the plastic strain in compression of the HIP-treated suction-cast alloy improved by about 22%, which is more than three times of the conventionally cast alloy.
For example, HIP treatment increases the yield strength of the suction-cast alloy at 1273 K from 388 MPa to 512 MPa.
